candidateDecisions.label: Quantitative pharmacology, drug movement and treatment evidence
candidateDecisions.reason: Drug action and kinetics provide the scientific anchor, supported by mathematical and computational methods for health research. The data courses teach transferable methods rather than clinical treatment decisions.

candidateDecisions.label: Patient-facing pharmacy and medicine-use practice
candidateDecisions.reason: Medical & Health Psychology studies consultation and shared decisions, and Ethics provides general normative reasoning. UCR lacks the formulation, dispensing and patient-specific medication review needed for a separate pharmacy practice option.

analysis: Both options are related academic responses grounded in drug action, kinetics, targets and adverse effects in Pharmacology, supported by biochemical and molecular mechanisms, organ-system physiology, disease cases and evidence synthesis. The closest adds human anatomy, infection and immunity, nervous-system foundations, health psychology and ethics. The laboratory course supplies hands-on protein, DNA and microbial techniques and interpretation. It complements research but does not substitute for pharmaceutical formulation or medicine quality control. The quantitative option adds linear algebra, advanced calculus, signals and linear systems, optimisation and neural networks. Numerical differential equations and uncertainty are relevant to concentration-response modelling, whereas filtering and generic machine learning contribute transferable methods. The programme does not claim that UCR teaches pharmacometric software or clinical prescribing. The 5 unique courses each way are 37.5 EC and give a different research emphasis. Human consultation and shared decision-making are substantive in Medical & Health Psychology, with Ethics adding responsibility and fairness. The available courses do not develop a patient-facing sequence in medication review, dispensing, formulation, pharmaceutical calculations or patient counselling. Meaningful overlap remains in scientific pharmaceutical concepts and research rather than pharmacy practice.
